title: Battle of Blue Licks, 1782: research notes
summary: Sourced fact outline behind the Battle of Blue Licks article: each side's aims, a dated timeline, casualties, people, contested claims and open questions.

sections.heading: British and Detroit Indian Department aims

items.text: Britain ran its western war from Detroit through the Indian Department, whose officers supplied, advised and often accompanied allied warriors.
Caldwell was sent west with about 50 Rangers after Clark took Vincennes; his commandant called him a very active partisan. In June 1782 his force defeated Crawford on the upper Sandusky.
Caldwell first meant to strike Wheeling, turned toward Kentucky after a false alarm that Clark was marching, and crossed the Ohio with three hundred Indians and Rangers.
McKee, a captain and interpreter with extensive influence among the Indians, took part in the attack on Bryan's Station.
Simon Girty was captured as a boy, raised among the Senecas and joined the British at Detroit in 1778. The DCB notes that a white savage legend grew from distortions of fact.
James and George Girty served Britain's Indian allies as interpreters, but no source in hand places either at Blue Licks.
Caldwell wrote that his warriors were Wyandots and Lake Indians and that the Wyandots supplied his provisions.
Kentucky and battlefield sources also name Shawnee and Delaware (Lenape) warriors.
In 1780 Indian leaders insisted that Bird's expedition turn up the Licking into Kentucky to face their old enemies the Kentucky settlers.

At Gnadenhutten in March 1782 Pennsylvania militia killed some 90 Christian Delawares; American Battlefield Trust says the massacre fed a desire for revenge in the Sandusky region. It is context for 1782, not a documented direct cause of Blue Licks.
Bryan's Station had just been besieged; buildings were burned and more than 300 hogs and 150 cattle killed.
Todd commanded; Trigg had the right, Boone the left, McGary the center and Harlan the advance.
Boone advised caution and a flanking move because of the ravines; the Kentuckians ignored his advice.
The tradition that McGary dared the men across shouting about cowards comes from later recollections and is not in Boone's 1782 letter or 1784 narrative.
Kentucky force: 176 (Filson), 181 (Boone), 182 (American Battlefield Trust).
British and Native force: about 200 in line (American Battlefield Trust); 300 crossed the Ohio and nearly 100 left before the battle (Caldwell); more than 400 guessed from trail sign (Boone).
Kentucky losses: 67 lost including 7 captured (Filson); about 70 killed (ExploreKYHistory); 77 killed and 12 wounded (Boone).
British and Native losses: one Ranger and six Indians killed, ten wounded (Caldwell). Caldwell claimed 146 killed and taken and wrongly listed Boone and McGary as dead.
Caldwell's Rangers returned to Detroit hardly capable of taking the field again, and the war moved to diplomacy.
In November 1782 Clark led Kentucky militia against the Shawnee towns on the Great Miami; the inhabitants left and five towns were burned.
The Treaty of Paris recognized U.S. independence and western bounds to the Mississippi; Native nations were not party to it.
A 32-acre battlefield tract became a state park and a 40-foot obelisk was unveiled August 19, 1928; it names the opposing nations but lists only Kentucky dead.
Trigg County (1820) and Todd County (1819) are named for the two fallen colonels.
Lack of means and authority to defend the district led Benjamin Logan to call the 1784 Danville meeting that began the conventions leading to statehood in 1792.

timeline.event: Mar. 8: Gnadenhutten massacre in the Ohio country
June: Caldwell and allies defeat Crawford on the upper Sandusky
Aug. 15 or 16: Caldwell's force surrounds Bryan's Station (Caldwell gives the 15th, Kentucky accounts the 16th)
Aug. 17: Attackers withdraw and camp at the Blue Licks
Aug. 18: About 180 militia pursue from Bryan's Station
Aug. 19: Battle of Blue Licks, about 15 minutes; militia routed (Caldwell dates it the 18th)
About Aug. 24: Logan's force of about 460 buries the dead; 43 found on the ground
Aug. 30: Boone asks Gov. Harrison for 500 men
Nov.: Clark's campaign burns five Shawnee towns on the Great Miami
Logan's Danville meeting on frontier defense begins the statehood conventions
